Can we store more logical qubits without making every check touch more data?

§

5.1 · What planar locality costs

Why does a rotated surface-code patch store only one logical qubit, however large its distance ddd grows? The rotated-patch count gives nine data and eight measure qubits at d=3d=3d=3. At d=5d=5d=5 it needs twenty-five data and twenty-four measure qubits, still for one logical qubit.

Is that cost specific to the surface code, or does any planar stabilizer code with bounded check reach pay it? Bounded reach means a fixed maximum separation between the qubits any check touches, even as the patch grows. Two things are at stake for the rest of this module: how many encoded qubits each data qubit can buy, and how far apart the qubits of one check may lie.

Multiplying by checks moves a logical operator without changing its encoded action. With bounded reach, we can push it off any region small enough to be correctable, a region whose loss still permits recovery. With a fixed limit on qubits per area, tiling a large patch with such regions leaves only small corner regions. Their Pauli labels must distinguish every logical Pauli action, and counting those labels gives the bound. We begin with one such move on the nine-qubit patch.

The logical Z on the top row can be moved to the bottom row. A logical representative is a physical operator that performs a particular encoded action.

Moving one operator is useful, but correctability requires every logical action to have a representative outside the region.

The X checks move it through X147(X1245X78)=X258X_{147}(X_{1245}X_{78})=X_{258}X147​(X1245​X78​)=X258​ and X258(X5689X23)=X369X_{258}(X_{5689}X_{23})=X_{369}X258​(X5689​X23​)=X369​. Thus both the Z row and X column avoid MMM.

For a stabilizer code, a correctable region contains no nontrivial logical Pauli. Losing that region therefore leaves enough information to recover any encoded state. The cleaning lemma states both directions: a region is correctable if and only if every logical Pauli has a representative outside it. The cleaning multiplication can use only generators touching the region A no-go theorem for a two-dimensional self-correcting quantum memory based on stabilizer codes, PDF p. 6, Lemma 1 Original source ↗ · DOI: 10.1088/1367-2630/11/4/043029.

This patch stores one qubit. Its logical X and Z generate all logical Pauli actions, including their product. Their outside representatives therefore certify that MMM is correctable. A moved Z alone would leave the X action unaccounted for.

Certify the region

For the nine-qubit rotated code with one encoded qubit, the region M={1,2,4,5}M=\{1,2,4,5\}M={1,2,4,5} is avoided by representatives Z789Z_{789}Z789​ and X369X_{369}X369​ of its logical Z and X. Hint

The logical Paulis are generated by logical X and Z.

Hint

The product of representatives supported outside MMM remains outside MMM.

Check against the rubric
  • Names X and Z as generators of all logical Pauli classes.
  • Explains why cleaning Z alone does not establish that X can be cleaned.
Show model solution

The logical identity already avoids MMM. The supplied X and Z representatives do too, so their product also acts only outside MMM. These generate every logical Pauli class of the encoded qubit. The cleaning lemma therefore certifies correctability.

A Z representative outside MMM alone does not establish that logical X can also avoid MMM. A nontrivial Z logical could still be supported inside MMM, obstructing that X cleaning. An X logical inside MMM would instead be impossible: it would have to anticommute with the disjoint outside Z. We need the complete set of logical actions, rather than a claim about the size of MMM.

Your rating schedules when to revisit this reasoning.

A check of fixed reach cannot touch well-separated tiles. This restriction lets us combine correctable regions on a larger patch.

A check is geometrically local when all the data qubits it touches fit within a fixed distance on the physical plane. Let www bound its reach, with the same bound throughout a growing family. Panel (a) separates the tiles far enough that no generator touches more than one tile.

Suppose a logical Pauli lies entirely in their union. Split its support into factors, one on each tile. Every generator sees at most one factor. Since the whole Pauli commutes with that generator, the factor must commute separately. Each factor is therefore a logical Pauli on a correctable tile, so it has trivial logical action. Their product is trivial too. The union contains no nontrivial logical and is correctable Quantum Information, Chapter 7: Quantum Error Correction (Ph219/CS219 lecture notes, updated March 2026), PDF p. 66 Original source ↗.

Two regions contain no nontrivial logical Pauli. What additional condition lets the local stabilizer union argument show that their union is correctable?

Hint: Factor a Pauli supported on the union into its two regional supports.

Your answer

A thin correctable shell can enlarge a correctable square. In panel (b), NNN is the correctable interior and KKK its new inner shell. The region SSS is the outer check boundary, containing any outside qubits reached by checks touching the enlarged square. Here SSS names a region, while S\mathcal SS still names the stabilizer group.

Choose KKK thick enough that no check touches both NNN and SSS. Under a fixed bound on data density, the fixed-width shell and boundary contain qubits in proportion to side length. They contain fewer than ddd qubits while that side stays below a suitable constant times ddd. Here ddd is the lightest nontrivial logical Pauli weight, so both regions are correctable.

Suppose a nontrivial logical fits in N∪KN\cup KN∪K. Clean it off KKK using generators touching KKK. Those generators can add support only inside N∪K∪SN\cup K\cup SN∪K∪S. The remaining logical lies in N∪SN\cup SN∪S, a separated correctable union. That is a contradiction Quantum Information, Chapter 7: Quantum Error Correction (Ph219/CS219 lecture notes, updated March 2026), PDF p. 67 Original source ↗.

Starting with a square containing fewer than ddd qubits, panel (c) repeats this growth.

Which parts grow like perimeter rather than area? The thin shell and outer check boundary do. They permit correctable squares with side proportional to ddd. Cutting corners from a correctable square preserves correctability: a logical in the subset would already fit in the square.

Only the small corner regions remain outside the tile collections in panel (d). Call the first collection AAA, the second BBB, and the remaining corner data CCC. Each collection is correctable by the separated-union argument. Clean AAA from a representative of every logical Pauli class. If two resulting representatives agree on CCC, their product lies in BBB. Correctability makes that product trivial, so the original classes were the same.

Thus different logical classes need different Pauli labels on CCC. Write ∣C∣|C|∣C∣ for the number of corner qubits. Each corner qubit offers four labels, I,X,Y,ZI,X,Y,ZI,X,Y,Z, just as each encoded qubit does. The 4k4^k4k logical classes must fit among at most 4∣C∣4^{|C|}4∣C∣ restrictions.

The BPT bound limits the product of the encoded-qubit count and squared distance for a planar code with bounded-range checks. Let nnn count data qubits, kkk encoded qubits, and ccc a locality-dependent constant. The notation OOO means an upper bound up to a fixed constant throughout the family. Derivation · Count the Pauli labels on the corners

Count restrictions after cleaning one collection. Choose one representative per logical Pauli class, each identity on AAA. Matching restrictions on CCC make their quotient supported on BBB, up to phase. Since BBB is correctable, that quotient is a stabilizer up to phase. The classes coincide. Consequently 4k≤4∣C∣4^k\leq4^{|C|}4k≤4∣C∣, hence k≤∣C∣k\leq|C|k≤∣C∣.

Fixed check reach makes each corner region constant in size. Tiles with side proportional to ddd occupy area proportional to d2d^2d2, giving ∣C∣=O(n/d2)|C|=O(n/d^2)∣C∣=O(n/d2). This geometric count assumes a planar lattice with bounded data density and bounded on-site Hilbert dimension. The commuting stabilizer checks have uniformly bounded geometric support diameter. The constant ccc depends on these bounds. This Pauli-label argument specializes the source’s geometric proof to stabilizer codes; it does not require cleaning AAA and then BBB without restoring support on AAA.

A long check can bridge the gap between the tiles. In panel (c), one generator touches separated pieces of a possible logical. Their anticommutation signs could cancel across the gap. We can no longer conclude that each piece commutes separately.

Check weight counts touched qubits. Physical range measures how far apart they lie. Surface codes already keep check weight bounded. The changed premise here is the fixed geometric range used in the planar-locality argument. The BPT bound assumes that range stays bounded, alongside finite data density and finite local Hilbert dimension.

Few neighbors, nearby neighbors?

A check touches six data qubits. Predict whether this tells us that all six lie within a fixed physical distance of each other as a family grows. Explain what information a list of six neighbors leaves out.

Six neighbors bounds check weight, but says nothing about their physical separation. A graph records incidence before a placement supplies distances. Compare your answer by naming the missing geometric data.

We can now identify the locality premise that makes the tile argument work. A graph can record check incidence without committing to positions on a chip.

5.2 · Few neighbors, wherever they are

The Hamming matrix already tells us which bits each parity check reads. Keep the column order from Module 2’s CSS construction, with bits labeled 111 through 777.

Panel (a) has rows a=1010101a=1010101a=1010101, b=0110011b=0110011b=0110011, and c=0001111c=0001111c=0001111. Row aaa tests whether the sum of bits 1,3,5,71,3,5,71,3,5,7 is even. A classical codeword is a bit string passing every parity check. A quantum code space also permits superpositions; these classical rows alone do not specify its quantum checks.

The Hamming matrix has seven columns and three independent rows, leaving four free bits. The repetition equations force three bits to share one value, leaving one free bit.

For a binary parity-check matrix HHH, let nnn count columns and let its rank count independent rows. Binary arithmetic, written GF(2)\mathrm{GF}(2)GF(2), adds modulo two. The dimension kclk_{\rm cl}kcl​ counts freely chosen information bits:

kcl=n−rank⁡GF(2)Hk_{\rm cl}=n-\operatorname{rank}_{\mathrm{GF}(2)} Hkcl​=n−rankGF(2)​H
(5.4)
Derivation · Count free bits by row elimination

Use binary row elimination to isolate a pivot variable for each independent equation. Every remaining variable is free, giving kcl=n−rank⁡Hk_{\rm cl}=n-\operatorname{rank}Hkcl​=n−rankH.

Count a check’s lines

In the Hamming matrix with first row 101010110101011010101 and columns 111 through 777, how many graph edges leave its first check?

Hint: Count ones in the row.

Explanation

The support is {1,3,5,7}\{1,3,5,7\}{1,3,5,7}, so the check has four incident edges. Each edge records one bit entering that parity sum.

One line from check aaa to bit 333 records one matrix entry. Panel (b) replaces every 111 in the matrix by a line while keeping the labels fixed. A Tanner graph draws one vertex for each data position, one for each check, and an edge wherever that check acts. The name honors Tanner A Recursive Approach to Low Complexity Codes Original source ↗ · DOI: 10.1109/TIT.1981.1056404.

Follow the lines from aaa: they end at 1,3,5,71,3,5,71,3,5,7, recovering its row. Moving the vertices changes the drawing without changing that row. Adding a redundant check instead changes the graph, even when the allowed codewords stay the same.

Read a row from the graph

A Tanner graph has one check adjacent to bits 2,3,6,72,3,6,72,3,6,7 among seven bits. Which matrix row does it represent?

Hint: Read the bits in the fixed order 111 through 777.

Your answer

Each bit in this next graph meets three checks, and each check meets six bits.

The design rate is the information fraction predicted by treating every written check row as independent. Dependencies can make the actual fraction larger.

Panel (a) partitions twelve bits into groups of six. The bit labels now run from 000 to 111111. Each group supplies a parity check, so every bit meets one check in this strip. Panel (b) adds strips with rearranged groups. A bit now participates once per strip, while each check still reads six bits.

The degree of a vertex is the number of edges incident to it. Here the bit degree is 333 and the check degree is 666. They are the column and row weights of the matrix, respectively. A family is low-density parity-check, or LDPC, when a choice of check matrices has bounded row and column weights as its size grows.

Gallager’s construction stacks such strips, permuting columns between them Low-Density Parity-Check Codes (monograph), PDF pp. 7, 13, Sections 1.2, 2.2 Original source ↗ · DOI: 10.7551/mitpress/4347.001.0001. We write jjj for his column weight and www for his row weight; his row-weight symbol is kkk. Our kkk remains the encoded dimension. This selected small member demonstrates fixed degrees. Its picture supplies no claim about typical distance in the larger ensemble.

A quantum LDPC family has stabilizer checks of bounded weight and bounded participation of each data qubit as the code grows. We abbreviate this as qLDPC. The toric and surface families already satisfy that definition: growing their lattices preserves the local check patterns and participation bounds. One finite Hamming or Steane matrix alone does not establish a family property.

Your answer

We can read sparsity from both row and column weights. Arbitrary sparse classical matrices need not satisfy the mixed-overlap condition; the product construction supplies the missing even overlaps.

5.3 · Build a quantum code from two classical graphs

Take the three-bit and two-bit repetition checks we can write by hand. Each check requires neighboring bits to agree. The allowed strings therefore repeat one freely chosen bit.

Thus Z(v0,d0)Z(v_0,d_0)Z(v0​,d0​) touches (v0,u0)(v_0,u_0)(v0​,u0​) and (v0,u1)(v_0,u_1)(v0​,u1​).

The check-pair positions C1×C2C_1\times C_2C1​×C2​ remain empty. This six-qubit candidate has both types of checks written down, but they still need to commute.

The first X check and the first Z check share only one qubit.

Panel (a) highlights their common position (v0,u0)(v_0,u_0)(v0​,u0​). At that qubit, interchanging X and Z contributes a minus sign. Every other factor commutes because it acts on a different qubit. The candidate checks therefore anticommute. They cannot both fix a nonzero state with eigenvalue +1+1+1: reversing their order would leave the state unchanged and also negate it.

A redundant row in a factor can contribute another logical degree of freedom. In the cyclic-factor inset, selecting all check rows gives a vanishing sum. A binary vector on check labels records this selection. Multiplication by HTH^THT tests whether the selected rows sum to zero.

Derivation · Count the product constraints

Count row dependencies before subtracting independent quantum constraints. The data sets contain n1n2n_1n_2n1​n2​ bit pairs and r1r2r_1r_2r1​r2​ check pairs, so n=n1n2+r1r2n=n_1n_2+r_1r_2n=n1​n2​+r1​r2​.

A dependency among X rows has one coefficient for each (ca,ub)(c_a,u_b)(ca​,ub​). Regard these coefficients as a vector in the product of the check-label space of factor one and bit-label space of factor two. The first column block vanishes when (H1T⊗In2)(H_1^T\otimes I_{n_2})(H1T​⊗In2​​) kills that vector. The second vanishes when (Ir1⊗H2)(I_{r_1}\otimes H_2)(Ir1​​⊗H2​) kills it.

Thus the first condition removes their coefficients, leaving only kernel directions in the first factor. For each remaining direction, the second condition requires its coefficient vector to lie in ker⁡H2\ker H_2kerH2​. Choosing a kernel basis there leaves k1Tk2k_1^Tk_2k1T​k2​ independent products of basis vectors. These are all X-row dependencies. Reversing the roles gives k1k2Tk_1k_2^Tk1​k2T​ Z-row dependencies. Explanation

Each dimension is 3−2=13-2=13−2=1. Therefore k=1⋅1+1⋅1=2k=1\cdot1+1\cdot1=2k=1⋅1+1⋅1=2. Dropping the transpose term would discard the contribution from paired row dependencies and miss one encoded qubit of the toric code.

A short factor string becomes a logical operator in the product. The dimension count alone does not tell us its weight.

Panel (b) adds X on {q0,q1}\{q_0,q_1\}{q0​,q1​}. It meets the first Z row twice and every other Z row zero times. Panel (c) adds Z on {q0,q2,q4}\{q_0,q_2,q_4\}{q0​,q2​,q4​}. Each X row meets it evenly. Both operators therefore commute with every check. They overlap each other only at q0q_0q0​, so they anticommute. Neither can be a stabilizer, which would commute with the other logical.

The X representative gives dX≤2d_X\leq2dX​≤2, and the Z representative gives dZ≤3d_Z\leq3dZ​≤3. The column band excludes smaller supports. Every column of both matrices is nonzero, so every weight-one Pauli has a nonzero syndrome. The HXH_XHX​ columns are also pairwise distinct, so no pair can sum to zero. No weight-two Z support passes every X check. Consequently dX=2d_X=2dX​=2, dZ=3d_Z=3dZ​=3, and the overall distance is d=2d=2d=2.

For general factors, let did_idi​ be the minimum nonzero word weight in ker⁡Hi\ker H_ikerHi​, and diTd_i^TdiT​ the corresponding transpose-code distance. A zero code has distance ∞\infty∞. (5.9)Starting model · tillich_zemor_hgp_2014
Derivation · Separate the drawn bounds from the theorem

Separate the drawn upper bounds from the theorem’s lower bound on all logical supports. In the small product, a Z error’s X syndrome is the sum of its selected HXH_XHX​ columns. Reading row 000 as the least significant bit, those columns are 1,2,5,10,4,8,3,121,2,5,10,4,8,3,121,2,5,10,4,8,3,12. None vanishes and no two match. Thus no weight-one or weight-two Z has zero syndrome. Nonzero HZH_ZHZ​ columns likewise exclude weight-one X; a single Y has both components and cannot evade the checks.

The pictured commuting pair has weights 222 and 333 and odd mutual overlap. It therefore attains dX=2d_X=2dX​=2 and dZ=3d_Z=3dZ​=3. A mixed logical contains a nontrivial X or Z component: otherwise both components would be stabilizers. Its union support cannot be lighter than that component, so the overall distance is 222.

For general factors, surviving factor strings supply upper bounds. The bound d≤did\leq d_id≤di​ requires a nonzero partner code, equivalently d3−i<∞d_{3-i}<\inftyd3−i​<∞. The bound d≤diTd\leq d_i^Td≤diT​ similarly requires d3−iT<∞d_{3-i}^T<\inftyd3−iT​<∞. Theorem 15 supplies the lower bound against every nontrivial logical; that general proof is imported here. Equality with the minimum follows when a minimizing term has a finite partner tillich_zemor_hgp_2014, PDF p. 15, Theorem 15 Original source ↗ · DOI: 10.1109/TIT.2013.2292061.

Full-row-rank factors have zero transpose codes, so their transpose distances are ∞\infty∞. With nonzero ordinary kernels, the partner condition gives d=min⁡(d1,d2)d=\min(d_1,d_2)d=min(d1​,d2​). Our open factors therefore give min⁡(3,2)=2\min(3,2)=2min(3,2)=2. For cyclic factors, all ordinary and transpose kernels are repetition codes of length LLL, so all four distances equal LLL. The partner condition gives d=Ld=Ld=L. A single drawn string would establish only the upper bound.

For the new cyclic L=3L=3L=3 instance in panels (d)–(f), the factor strings become three-site logical representatives. The theorem excludes shorter ones, giving d=3d=3d=3.

Method: Form the binary shift matrices, then join blocks to form HXH_XHX​ and HZH_ZHZ​. Row reduction uses binary addition. Tolerances: Binary operations and integer counts have no rounding tolerance. Geometry only positions the drawing and does not determine a code parameter.

Display conventions

  • The two sheets use the same coordinate scale. X support is solid amber; Z support is dashed teal. Detached markers denote the two checks.
  • Hop labels give exponents, including long hops. Paired boundary arrowheads mark a periodic seam crossing. Halos show shared support, not a coupling between data sites.
  • Focus starts at X(0,0) and Z(1,1). The adjacent support lists remain readable at larger sizes.
  • All controls use counts, indices or binary polynomial choices. Numeric inputs round to integers and clamp to the stated range before focus indices wrap. Nonfinite or missing numbers use the default.

Tangent: why polynomial multiplication describes hops

Optional. A group algebra is a binary vector space whose basis labels are group elements and whose multiplication follows the group law. Here those labels are pairs of cyclic indices. Multiplying labels adds coordinates; distributing products adds the contributions to each resulting hop. This is convolution with binary coefficients. The relations xℓ=1x^\ell=1xℓ=1, ym=1y^m=1ym=1 describe the finite torus, and transpose reverses each translation. We keep the shift dimensions of PDF p. 7 when reading the notation on p. 23 High-threshold and low-overhead fault-tolerant quantum memory, PDF pp. 7, 23 Original source ↗ · DOI: 10.1038/s41586-024-07107-7.

Count the full neighborhood

One BB data qubit belongs to 333 X checks and 333 Z checks. How many direct check-data couplings would its full Tanner neighborhood require?

Hint: Count the two check types together.

Explanation

The full neighborhood has six incidences. Dividing it into two degree-three layers does not reduce the total required neighbors.

Label the hop terms in written order: A1,A2,A3A_1,A_2,A_3A1​,A2​,A3​ and B1,B2,B3B_1,B_2,B_3B1​,B2​,B3​. Split their edges while retaining every vertex.

Panel (b) assigns A2,A3,B3A_2,A_3,B_3A2​,A3​,B3​ to layer aaa and A1,B1,B2A_1,B_1,B_2A1​,B1​,B2​ to layer bbb. Each vertex has degree three per layer, six in their union. Both layers contain X and Z checks.

Graph thickness is the smallest number of planar edge layers whose union is the graph. Panels (c) and (d)’s paired cycles and radial matching edges prove thickness at most two. Let VVV contain all Tanner vertices and EEE all incidence edges; ⊔\sqcup⊔ means a disjoint union:

E=Ea⊔Eb,Ga=(V,Ea),Gb=(V,Eb) are planarE=E_a\sqcup E_b,\qquad G_a=(V, E_a),\quad G_b=(V, E_b)\text{ are planar}E=Ea​⊔Eb​,Ga​=(V,Ea​),Gb​=(V,Eb​) are planar

Derivation · Expose the cycles by removing the matching

Remove the matching edges to expose the cycles. In layer aaa, remove B3B_3B3​; the remaining edges alternate A2,A3A_2,A_3A2​,A3​. In layer bbb, remove A1A_1A1​; the cycles alternate B1,B2B_1,B_2B1​,B2​. Commuting translations make the matching preserve neighboring positions on the paired cycles. Draw the cycles on concentric polygons and restore the matching radially. No edges cross within either drawing High-threshold and low-overhead fault-tolerant quantum memory, PDF pp. 9-11, Lemma 2, Fig. 3 Original source ↗ · DOI: 10.1038/s41586-024-07107-7.

For the tiny instance, each layer has 363636 edges and two components, each containing two six-vertex cycles. For gross, each layer has 432432432 edges. Layer aaa has twelve components with twelve vertices per cycle; layer bbb has six components with twenty-four vertices per cycle. Together the layers contain all 864864864 edges. This constructs an upper bound of two, without proving minimality.

The paper calls this a thickness-two layout. Its cycle order counts two-edge moves, rather than individual vertices. Physical routing also requires common positions and fabrication constraints. Mathews and colleagues describe proposed HAL layouts. Their proposed gross-code layout uses five tiers in total: the qubit tier and four higher routing tiers. This count applies to that placement; it is not a universal minimum Placing and routing quantum LDPC codes in multilayer superconducting hardware, PDF pp. 4-5, Fig. 3, Table I Original source ↗ · DOI: 10.1038/s41534-026-01243-w.

Initial conditions
The gross graph starts in planar-grid layout with the long-edge readout, cutoff one, and X check zero selected. No time evolution or initial quantum state is modeled.
Boundary conditions
Matrix indices wrap modulo ℓ\ellℓ and mmm. Drawings are unwrapped; every segment joins its displayed endpoints without wrapping across the screen.
Required connections in the selected placement
All required edges in fixed placements, two separate sheets in thickness mode, or six active edges with all others pending. Lengths have no physical meaning in the independent layer sheets. Readouts give scope, long edges, strict crossings, overlaps, vertex contacts, and host-native connections where applicable. Horizontal: Horizontal drawing coordinate (drawing pitch units). Vertical: Vertical drawing coordinate (drawing pitch units).
Displayed incidence edges
Start at zero and count displayed edges through all X checks followed by all Z checks. Full tiny ends at 72 edges over 12 checks; full gross ends at 864 over 144. One active neighborhood ends at six. Horizontal: Check vertices included, t (checks). Vertical: Displayed incidence edges c(t) (edges).

Method: Form binary shift matrices locally and attach the generating term to every incidence edge. Assign the fixed toric grid or the first host vertices ordered by vertical then horizontal coordinate. Measure Euclidean lengths and strict segment intersections. Diagnose positive collinear overlap and edges containing unrelated vertices separately. For each layer, remove its declared matching, traverse both cycles, and check that the matching preserves cycle adjacency before drawing them.

Tolerances: Binary matrices and graph counts use integer arithmetic. Strict crossings require both orientation products below -1e-12. Contact predicates use 1e-9; squared lengths within 1e-12 of the cutoff are equal for floating-point comparisons.

Display conventions

  • X edges are solid and Z edges dashed. Squares mark checks; circles mark data. The selected X check and its six data neighbors are emphasized, with their IDs listed beside the drawing.
  • Thickness mode draws each paired cycle on concentric polygons of radii two and one. Matching edges join corresponding vertices radially. Component tiles are spaced five drawing units apart; the two sheets have independent coordinates.
  • The metric menu emphasizes a readout. In fixed placements, the threshold changes which edges count as long. No distances are normalized by the number of vertices.
  • Other required connections pending. The active view displays a neighborhood, not a movement schedule.

Normalize the distance

The source-reported BB72 parameters are n=72n=72n=72 and d=6d=6d=6. What is the relative distance d/nd/nd/n, as a decimal to three significant figures?

Hint: Reduce the ratio 6/726/726/72.

Explanation

The relative distance is 6/72=1/126/72=1/126/72=1/12. This finite ratio is not a claim about a family limit.

A growing family must keep both ratios positive to preserve their benefits at larger sizes. A code family is asymptotically good when its rate and relative distance both stay bounded away from zero as its size grows. The lower bounds may depend on the family. They must hold for all sufficiently large members, not just selected finite examples. The notation lim inf⁡\liminfliminf expresses those eventual lower bounds:

lim inf⁡n→∞R>0,lim inf⁡n→∞δ>0\liminf_{n\to\infty} R>0,\qquad\liminf_{n\to\infty}\delta>0n→∞liminf​R>0,n→∞liminf​δ>0

Derivation · Separate the quantifiers from the toy example

Separate the theorem’s quantifiers from the toy’s local identity. Theorem 2 permits each fixed target R0∈(0,1)R_0\in(0,1)R0​∈(0,1) and supplies an explicit qLDPC family with unbounded size. Check weights and data participation remain bounded across that family. Its statement d=Θ(n)d=\Theta(n)d=Θ(n) includes a lower bound d≥δ0nd\ge\delta_0nd≥δ0​n for a fixed positive construction-dependent δ0\delta_0δ0​ Asymptotically Good Quantum and Locally Testable Classical LDPC Codes, PDF p. 3, Theorem 2 Original source ↗ · DOI: 10.1145/3519935.3520017.

The theorem requires global connections and algebraic choices absent from our cyclic example. We import its existence proof; agreement of two drawn routes does not prove it. The constants describe a suitable family, not parameters assignable to an arbitrary finite BB code.

Can the three-copy example certify δ0\delta_0δ0​? No: it supplies no bound on all nontrivial logical supports.

Put data qubits on the square faces of a three-column, two-row chart.

A square complex joins vertices and edges with square faces whose boundaries follow those edges. In panel (a), u=v11u=v_{11}u=v11​ belongs to vertex set V1V_1V1​, while its neighbor v=v21v=v_{21}v=v21​ belongs to V0V_0V0​. These labels follow the source convention. Neither vertex carries a check yet.

Each vertex sees four incident faces. At uuu, the ordered local matrix is Wu=[q00q01q10q11]W_u=\begin{bmatrix}q_{00}&q_{01}\\q_{10}&q_{11}\end{bmatrix}Wu​=[q00​q10​​q01​q11​​]; at vvv, it is Wv=[q10q11q20q21]W_v=\begin{bmatrix}q_{10}&q_{11}\\q_{20}&q_{21}\end{bmatrix}Wv​=[q10​q20​​q11​q21​​]. They share q10q_{10}q10​ and q11q_{11}q11​ Quantum Tanner codes, PDF pp. 2, 6, 18, Fig. 2 Original source ↗ · DOI: 10.1109/focs54457.2022.00117.

Panel (b) adds an X constraint at uuu. Choose short codes CA=CB=span⁡{11}C_A=C_B=\operatorname{span}\{11\}CA​=CB​=span{11}. The span consists of binary sums of the given row. A binary dual code contains words orthogonal to every word of the original code. Here orthogonality to 111111 requires equal entries, so CA⊥=CB⊥=span⁡{11}C_A^\perp=C_B^\perp=\operatorname{span}\{11\}CA⊥​=CB⊥​=span{11}.

Use the Kronecker product already defined for matrices. Replace each entry of 111111 by that entry times the row 111111, giving 111111111111. Its binary span is {0000,1111}\{0000,1111\}{0000,1111}, the code CA⊥⊗CB⊥C_A^\perp\otimes C_B^\perpCA⊥​⊗CB⊥​. We use 111111111111 as the X-check row. In the global face order, this gives HZ=001111H_Z=001111HZ​=001111. Its allowed local words form DZ=(CA⊗CB)⊥D_Z=(C_A\otimes C_B)^\perpDZ​=(CA​⊗CB​)⊥.

A quantum Tanner code uses this local-code prescription on a suitable square complex. The source assigns Z generators from CA⊗CBC_A\otimes C_BCA​⊗CB​ to V0V_0V0​, and X generators from CA⊥⊗CB⊥C_A^\perp\otimes C_B^\perpCA⊥​⊗CB⊥​ to V1V_1V1​. Our six-face chart demonstrates that prescription locally. It does not satisfy a good-family theorem merely by having compatible rows Quantum Tanner codes, PDF p. 18, Eq. 4 Original source ↗ · DOI: 10.1109/focs54457.2022.00117.

A small cluster can evade distant constraints if its vertices have too few neighbors outside the cluster. Expansion requires sufficiently small vertex sets to have many neighbors outside themselves, with a fixed lower bound proportional to set size.

The quantum Tanner theorem combines suitable expansion with robust local-code conditions. Those conditions control how local row and column constraints combine, including under restricted neighborhoods. The repetition-code example teaches compatibility; it does not establish those conditions. Leverrier and Zémor prove that suitable choices exist, giving another family with positive rate and linear distance Quantum Tanner codes, PDF pp. 2, 24, Theorem 18 Original source ↗ · DOI: 10.1109/focs54457.2022.00117.

Tangent: degree is not expansion

Optional. In the lifted-edge picture, the three edges still form three disconnected components. Take the two vertices of one whole component. They have no neighbors outside that set, despite bounded degree. A lift alone therefore does not ensure expansion. The quantum Tanner theorem needs quantified global expansion together with suitable local-code conditions Quantum Tanner codes, PDF pp. 1-2, 24 Original source ↗ · DOI: 10.1109/focs54457.2022.00117.

Hint

Check against the rubric

Show model solution

A long check may touch regions previously separated by more than the check reach. Regional pieces of a commuting Pauli need no longer commute separately, so the correctable-union proof can fail. This removes that proof of the upper bound. It establishes no lower bound on kkk or ddd.

The added stabilizers must still commute. Their independent rank determines the new kkk, while a family-wide bound on all nontrivial logical supports is needed for linear ddd. Sparse incidence alone supplies neither claim.

Adding commuting rows on the same data block cannot decrease stabilizer rank. Thus k=n−rank⁡HX−rank⁡HZk=n-\operatorname{rank}H_X-\operatorname{rank}H_Zk=n−rankHX​−rankHZ​ cannot increase. An enlarging single-patch family already has vanishing rate, so adding checks alone cannot give it positive constant rate. Escaping a bound’s premise is not a construction achieving the desired parameters.

The selected check shares (1,3)(1,3)(1,3) and (0,0)(0,0)(0,0) with fff. Two overlaps give even parity, so the operators commute. The logical partner shares only (0,0)(0,0)(0,0), giving odd parity and anticommutation. A stabilizer commutes with every valid logical partner, so XfX_fXf​ cannot be a stabilizer.

The support contains 8+4=128+4=128+4=12 sites. Together with its zero syndrome, it gives d≤12d\le12d≤12. Testing this one check alone does not establish that XfX_fXf​ commutes with every check. The source construction supplies that fact through Bf=0Bf=0Bf=0, as explained in the logical-support derivation. The equality d=12d=12d=12 remains the separate source-reported distance.

Break the six-neighbor claim

The statement “three terms in AAA and three in BBB give six neighbors for every torus size” omits an assumption. On ℓ=3\ell=3ℓ=3, m=2m=2m=2, take A=x3+y+y2A=x^3+y+y^2A=x3+y+y2 and B=y3+x+x2B=y^3+x+x^2B=y3+x+x2. Reduce both polynomials using periodicity and binary addition. Find the check weight, and explain whether commutation HXHZT=0H_XH_Z^T=0HX​HZT​=0 still follows.

Hint

x3=1x^3=1x3=1 and y2=1y^2=1y2=1.

Hint

Repeated monomials cancel; the remaining shifts still commute.

Check against the rubric
  • Reduces AAA to yyy and BBB to y+x+x2y+x+x^2y+x+x2.
  • Obtains check weight four and identifies lost distinctness.
  • Retains CSS commutation because the reduced translations commute.
Show model solution

Periodicity gives A=1+y+1=yA=1+y+1=yA=1+y+1=y. Also y3=yy^3=yy3=y, so B=y+x+x2B=y+x+x^2B=y+x+x2, with three distinct terms. An X check has one LLL neighbor and three RRR neighbors, for weight four. The reversed, exchanged Z construction also has weight four.

The omitted assumption was distinct translations after reduction modulo the torus periods. The remaining shifts still commute, so AB+BA=0AB+BA=0AB+BA=0 continues to guarantee CSS commutation. The two-block construction remains valid, while the claimed six-neighbor form fails.
